explanations: luna: The section’s root note for ظ ه ر treats backing as support; this ayah condemns people who “تَظَاهَرُونَ عَلَيْهِمْ بِالْإِثْمِ وَالْعُدْوَانِ,” so mutual support can add wrongdoing rather than lift a burden. | terra: The Israelites “support one another” in sin and aggression against part of their own people, an unethical collective form of the source's backing relation.
terra: The dominion of heavens and earth belongs to Allah, and no protector or helper exists apart from Him; sovereignty and exclusive refuge meet explicitly.
terra: In the fasting ruling God explicitly desires ease rather than hardship for people, a legal instance of the Lord easing a duty.
terra: In allocating parents' nursing and maintenance duties, the ayah says no soul is charged beyond its capacity, a specific boundary on assigned family burdens.

luna: The section presents God taking a burden off the addressee; this closing plea asks “وَلَا تُحَمِّلْنَا مَا لَا طَاقَةَ لَنَا بِهِ,” making the need for divine release from an unbearable load explicit. | terra: The prayer asks God not to lay on the believers an إِصْرًا, not to make them carry what exceeds capacity, and ends “You are our protector”; burden relief and refuge meet in one appeal.
terra: Calling God “Owner of dominion” distinguishes the absolute sovereign from rulers whose authority and burdens are granted and removed by Him.
terra: Mary's mother entrusts her and her offspring to God's refuge from Satan, extending protection to one who cannot yet seek it herself.
terra: After Zechariah's prayer is answered, he is told to remember his Lord much and glorify morning and evening; a granted request likewise issues in abundant remembrance and tasbih.
terra: Jesus asks who will be his helpers toward Allah and the disciples volunteer, a prophetic-mission parallel to Moses requesting a human supporter for God's work.

luna: The section defines Rabb as owner and obeyed master while directing the reader to God; this call rejects taking one another as “أَرْبَابًا مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ,” setting a limit on human claims to that authority. | terra: The shared word calls people not to take one another as arbāb apart from Allah, setting the boundary between human masters and the true Lord.
terra: No prophet commands people to take angels or prophets as lords, excluding exalted servants from the master's place.

luna: The section describes angels as supporters and the final appeal to the Rabb; this ayah asks whether it is enough that their Lord reinforce them with three thousand angels, a direct parallel of help sent by the Lord. | terra: The Prophet asks whether reinforcement by three thousand angels will suffice the believers, a specific angelic-backing scene.

luna: Continuing the reinforcement in 3:124, this ayah promises five thousand angels if the believers are patient and mindful; it adds the stated condition for the Lord’s support. | terra: Steadfastness and reverence are answered with a promise of five thousand marked angels, completing the offered reinforcement.
terra: Allah, rather than feared human enemies, is the believers' Protector and the best of helpers, directly naming the source image's true supporting master.

luna: The section’s dictionary describes a vizier as one whose judgment a ruler relies on; here the Prophet is told to consult the believers in a matter and then rely on God when resolved, giving a direct scene of leadership using counsel before turning to God. | terra: The Prophet is told to consult companions in the affair, but after deciding to rely on Allah, distinguishing valued human counsel from ultimate dependence on the Lord.
terra: God desires to lighten the human burden because the human was created weak, a direct statement of the Lord's relieving action.

luna: The section’s helper and refuge images meet in this plea from the oppressed: they ask God to appoint “وَلِيًّا” and “نَصِيرًا” from Himself, making protection and support a response to people who cannot release themselves.

luna: The section’s lexicon calls a mountain a refuge one flees to; this ayah says death reaches people “فِي بُرُوجٍ مُّشَيَّدَةٍ” (fortified towers), marking the limit of physical fortifications as refuge. | terra: Death overtakes people even inside lofty fortified towers, setting a limit on every material shelter named by the source's broad refuge definition.
terra: The command to cooperate in righteousness but not in sin gives an explicit ethical rule for when people should or should not act as one another's support.
terra: After ablution rules, God says He does not intend hardship but purification, a concrete legal instance of the Lord refusing an onerous load.

terra: Abel tells his aggressor that he will bear both the sin against him and his own sin, a moral-causation exception that clarifies how one person's act can add to another's load without substitution.

luna: The section’s root note links وِزْر to a load that made the back creak; this ayah pictures people “أَوْزَارَهُمْ عَلَىٰ ظُهُورِهِمْ” carrying burdens on their backs, a judgment scene that reverses the relief of 94:2–3. | terra: They carry their أَوْزَارَهُمْ on their ظُهُورِهِمْ, placing the source section's burden and back together in one literalized judgment scene.

luna: The section recalls Moses asking for his chest to be opened; this ayah describes God expanding a person’s chest toward Islam and, in contrast, making it tight and constricted, extending the same bodily image to guidance and resistance.
terra: The command concerning an orphan's property and just measure is qualified by charging no soul beyond capacity, limiting what the Master requires.

luna: The section’s dictionary root و ز ر describes one bearer taking a load off another; this ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى,” limiting that image when the load is each soul’s moral liability. | terra: “No burden-bearer bears another's burden” sets the accountability boundary against the source dictionary's minister who voluntarily carries his principal's load; the ayah also ends with return to the Lord.

luna: The section’s dictionary explicitly links ittizār, wearing a waist-wrap, to و ز ر; this ayah describes clothing that covers nakedness and adorns people, a concrete garment parallel for that secondary sense, though it does not use the word izār. | terra: Clothing that covers nakedness supplies a plausible Quranic garment counterpart to the source dictionary's ittizār or tied waistcloth branch, though the ayah uses neither the garment form nor the و ز ر root.
terra: The promise to believing doers is introduced by the rule that no soul is charged beyond capacity, another repeated formulation of measured obligation.
terra: Thamud carve homes in the mountains after being settled in the land, another mountain-as-habitation scene, though refuge from an immediate threat is not stated.

luna: The section’s minister is a helper who carries another’s work; Moses tells Aaron “اخْلُفْنِي فِي قَوْمِي” and to set things right, showing Aaron entrusted to stand in for him during his absence. | terra: Moses appoints Aaron as his deputy among the people and commands him to set matters right, a functional minister scene that also activates the source definition of rabb as one who reforms.

luna: The section describes God removing the addressee’s load; here the messenger “يَضَعُ عَنْهُمْ إِصْرَهُمْ” and their shackles, a parallel image of a divinely sent helper relieving people’s burden. | terra: The Messenger “puts off them” their burden and shackles, closely matching the source section's وَضَعْنَا عَنكَ relation even though the noun here is إصر.
terra: Those invoked apart from Allah can neither help their callers nor help themselves, exposing false supporters' incapacity.
terra: When satanic provocation comes, the addressee is commanded to seek refuge in Allah, turning spiritual attack into the same action of flight to divine shelter.

luna: The section brings together a helper and the final turn to the Rabb, and also describes angels as supporters; here believers call their Lord for help and He answers by reinforcing them with a thousand angels, joining divine response and angelic support in one scene. | terra: God answers the believers' plea for help by reinforcing them with successive angels, an enacted parallel to the angelic support named in 66:4.
luna: Following the angelic reinforcement in 8:9, this ayah says the angels are reassurance for believers’ hearts and that victory comes only from God; it clarifies the support’s source and purpose.
terra: If opponents turn away, believers are reminded that Allah is their Protector, “excellent Protector and excellent Helper.”
terra: Allah is sufficient for the Prophet and is the One who strengthened him with divine victory and the believers, combining the true support with human supporters.
terra: Allah is declared sufficient for the Prophet and for the believers who follow him, another same-addressee statement that the Lord supplies His servants' support.
terra: God explicitly lightens the believers' obligation after knowing their weakness, showing the master adjusting the servant's load.
terra: Those who gave refuge and support are paired with the emigrants as mutual protectors, combining shelter and active backing in one community relation.
terra: The repeated description “gave refuge and supported” makes hospitality and help the defining action of true believers.
terra: Faithfulness to treaty partners is conditioned on their not supporting anyone against the believers, showing support as an alliance-defining act.

luna: The section’s root ر ب ب includes the obeyed master; this ayah says people took their scholars and monks as “أَرْبَابًا مِّن دُونِ اللَّهِ,” a concrete warning against misplaced obedience. | terra: Taking scholars and monks as lords besides Allah exemplifies the source dictionary's “obeyed master” sense misdirected toward creatures.

luna: The section joins a refuge with a supporter who steadies another; in this cave scene the Prophet reassures his companion that God is with them, and God sends down tranquility and unseen aid, meeting both parts of the image. | terra: In the cave the Prophet is told not to grieve because Allah is with the two, after which divine tranquility and unseen forces support him.

luna: The section names the refuge sense of the root و ز ر; these people would rush toward any “مَلْجَأٍ” or cave (“مَغَارَاتٍ”) they could find, showing the flight to an earthly shelter that contrasts with the section’s turn to God. | terra: The hypocrites would bolt toward a refuge, caves, or any entrance if they found one, a physical flight-to-shelter scene without the source section's Lordward correction.
terra: Allah owns the heavens and earth, gives life and death, and people have no protector or helper apart from Him.

luna: The section’s general dictionary gloss for و ز ر is anything one seeks refuge in; here the earth narrows and they realize “أَن لَّا مَلْجَأَ مِنَ اللَّهِ إِلَّا إِلَيْهِ,” making God the sole refuge. | terra: The three discover that there is no مَلْجَأَ from Allah except to Him, the paradoxical refuge-in-the-One-from-whom-one-cannot-flee developed by the section.
terra: The Prophet is told to declare Allah sufficient, trust in Him, and name Him Lord of the mighty Throne, a direct stance of reliance on the sovereign Lord.

luna: The section’s dictionary explicitly calls the root و ز ر a mountain one flees to for refuge; Noah’s son says “سَآوِي إِلَىٰ جَبَلٍ يَعْصِمُنِي مِنَ الْمَاءِ,” but the mountain cannot save him. | terra: Noah's son says he will seek refuge on a mountain that will protect him, but no protector exists from God's command except His mercy; the dictionary's refuge-mountain is explicitly overruled.

luna: The section’s lexicon gives Rabb the secondary gloss “one who sets things right”; Shuaib says he seeks reform as far as he can, that his success is only through God, and that he relies on and turns to Him, concretely linking reform with dependence on God. | terra: Shuayb seeks only reform, says his success is through Allah, relies on Him, and turns to Him; this concretely unites the source definitions of reformer, reliance, and Lordward direction.
terra: Shuayb asks whether his clan is mightier than Allah and rebukes his people for putting God behind their backs, reversing the back as a place of relied-upon support.

luna: The section’s dictionary defines ر ب ب as owner and obeyed master as well as Lord; Joseph calls the household owner “رَبِّي” when refusing to betray him, illustrating the human-master sense. | terra: Joseph seeks refuge in Allah when solicited; his following use of rabb has a known master/Lord ambiguity, so the ayah also exposes the human-master and divine-Lord senses without safely collapsing them.
terra: Joseph contrasts divided human lords with Allah, the One and Overpowering, making the lexical master sense a theological choice.
terra: Rule belongs only to Allah and worship is commanded for Him alone, explaining why creaturely masters cannot occupy the final refuge of the source image.

luna: The section names ر ب ب as master and owner; in Joseph’s prison interpretation one servant “فَيَسْقِي رَبَّهُ خَمْرًا,” using the word for an earthly master. | terra: Joseph uses rabb for the cupbearer's human master, directly exemplifying the source dictionary's nondivine “master” sense.

luna: The section’s human-master sense of ر ب ب appears when Joseph asks the released servant “اذْكُرْنِي عِندَ رَبِّكَ”; the servant is to appeal to the king who holds authority over him. | terra: “Mention me to your lord” again uses rabb for the royal master and places a close court servant between a petitioner and the ruler.

luna: The section echoes “to your Rabb” as the destination of turning; Joseph is told “ارْجِعْ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ” about the women, where Rabb means the earthly king, clarifying the master sense beside the divine address. | terra: The command “return to your lord” uses rabb for the king, another clear Quranic instance of the title's human-master sense.
terra: The king reserves Joseph for himself and declares him established and trusted, a functional court analogue to the dependable adviser in the source definition of minister.
terra: Joseph asks to be placed over the land's storehouses, specifying the entrusted public burden that follows his admission to the king's confidence.

luna: The section’s dictionary says a person’s “back” can mean their supporters; this ayah pictures successive guardians before and behind a person, protecting them by God’s command. The link is an indirect protection scene rather than shared wording. | terra: When Allah intends harm for a people it cannot be repelled, and they have no protecting patron apart from Him.
terra: Thamud carve houses from the mountains while feeling secure, a direct Quranic realization of the mountain as protective shelter.
terra: God acknowledges that the Prophet's breast is constricted by what opponents say, providing a precise reversal against the opened breast in surah 94.
terra: The answer to the constricted breast of 15:97 is to glorify the Lord with praise and prostrate, linking strain to the same Lordward tasbih sought in Moses' prayer.

luna: The section’s dictionary root و ز ر pictures a helper taking a load away; this ayah says misleaders bear “مِنْ أَوْزَارِ الَّذِينَ يُضِلُّونَهُمْ,” an opposite case where leading others astray adds to one’s own burden. | terra: Misleaders bear their own burdens and some burdens arising from those they mislead; this qualifies nontransfer by moral causation rather than a helper taking guilt away.

luna: The section’s dictionary gloss for و ز ر includes both a mountain refuge and anything one fortifies oneself with; this ayah says God made “أَكْنَانًا” in mountains and protective “سَرَابِيلَ,” joining shelter and bodily protection in one provision. | terra: God makes mountain shelters and protective garments for people, uniquely joining the source dictionary's mountain-refuge and girded-garment branches in one ayah.
terra: Before reciting the Quran the addressee is commanded to seek refuge in Allah from Satan, placing refuge at the threshold of the weighty revealed word.

luna: The section quotes Moses asking God to open his chest for his mission; this ayah uses the same chest-opening wording for someone who opens their breast to disbelief, showing the image’s contrary direction.

luna: The section’s root و ز ر names a burden, but here “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى” says moral guilt is not transferred from one soul to another; relief from one’s load has a personal-accountability boundary. | terra: Each person's guidance or error falls on that person and no bearer carries another's burden, limiting the helper metaphor in moral judgment.
terra: The prayer for parents recalls “as they reared me when small,” a creaturely instance of the nurturing sense behind the source definition of rabb as reformer.
terra: Even if humans and jinn were ظَهِيرًا to one another, they could not produce the Quran's like; the helper word is used for total mutual backing.
terra: The Prophet praises the King who has no partner in rule and no protecting ally arising from weakness, explicitly rejecting neediness in the divine sovereign.

luna: The section’s dictionary root note broadens refuge to whatever one seeks shelter and protection in; these youths “أَوَى الْفِتْيَةُ إِلَى الْكَهْفِ” and pray to their Lord for mercy, a concrete sanctuary scene. | terra: The youths take refuge in the cave and ask their Lord to grant mercy and prepare right conduct in their affair, joining mountain shelter, Lordward prayer, and a made-fit task.

luna: The section’s dictionary broadens refuge to whatever one seeks shelter and protection in; these youths are told to take refuge in the cave, where their Lord will spread mercy and prepare ease for their affair, combining sanctuary with divine relief. | terra: Retreat to the cave is followed by the promise that the Lord will spread mercy and prepare مِرْفَقًا in their affair, making divine shelter also practical facilitation.
terra: No one can alter the Lord's words, and the addressee will find no مُلْتَحَدًا apart from Him; the Lord is the sole refuge.
terra: The garden owner has no company to support him apart from Allah and cannot defend himself, showing worldly backing collapse at the point of need.
terra: God says He never took the misleaders as an عَضُدًا, an arm-support image that denies any need for corrupt helpers and parallels the arm strengthened in 28:35.
terra: For the appointed reckoning the wrongdoers will find no مَوْئِلًا, another explicit denial of refuge in judgment.
terra: Dhu al-Qarnayn asks the people to help him with strength in building the barrier, a leader sharing a difficult public task with supporters.
terra: Mary seeks refuge in the Merciful from the unknown visitor, a concrete human-threat scene of taking divine shelter.
terra: Giving Moses his brother Aaron as a prophet “from Our mercy” presents the supportive brother as a divine gift, though it does not call him minister here.
terra: God says He made revelation easy in the Prophet's tongue so he can give good news and warning, meeting Moses' requests for eased speech and effective mission.
terra: God tells the Prophet that the Quran was not sent down to make him suffer, a same-addressee denial that the Lord's revelation is meant as a crushing load.

luna: The section notes that Moses’ plea for a helper follows his request for an opened chest; he begins “رَبِّ اشْرَحْ لِي صَدْرِي,” the same need for inward opening before a difficult task. | terra: Moses first asks his Lord to expand his breast, beginning the sequence that the source section aligns with surah 94 before the request for a minister.

luna: The section places Moses’ request for a vizier beside his request for ease; “وَيَسِّرْ لِي أَمْرِي” states the task-relief that the helper is meant to make possible. | terra: “Ease my affair” supplies the second step of the breast–ease–minister–remembrance sequence developed in the source prose.
terra: The request to untie the knot from Moses' tongue supplies the limitation that makes Aaron's greater eloquence and confirming support in 28:34 intelligible.
terra: Moses asks that people understand his speech, completing the speech problem immediately before he requests a minister.

luna: The section’s dictionary root و ز ر connects the burden removed in 94:2 with a human helper who carries for another; Moses asks, “وَزِيرًا مِّنْ أَهْلِي,” explicitly naming that supporting role. | terra: Moses explicitly asks his Lord for a وَزِيرًا; this is the Quranic enactment of the source dictionary's burden-bearing helper.

luna: The section quotes Moses asking for a family vizier in 20:29; this next ayah names “هَارُونَ أَخِي,” identifying the brother who will carry the supporting role. | terra: Naming “Aaron, my brother” identifies the family member who will embody the requested minister in 20:29.

luna: The section links a helper with the back as a place of support; Moses asks “اشْدُدْ بِهِ أَزْرِي.” The section explicitly notes that أَزْرِي is a different root from و ز ر, while the bodily image still meets the helper who strengthens him. | terra: Moses asks that Aaron strengthen his أَزْرِي; this bodily support image is the source section's explicit parallel to a helper bracing one's back, while أزر is a distinct root from وزر.

luna: After asking for Aaron and strength in 20:29–31, Moses asks “وَأَشْرِكْهُ فِي أَمْرِي”; this ayah’s contribution is shared work, not only borrowed strength. | terra: “Make him share in my affair” states the partnership by which the minister takes part in his principal's task.

luna: The section says Moses’ helper is requested so they can glorify God; this next part of the same prayer gives that purpose as “كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا.” | terra: Moses gives abundant glorification as the purpose of receiving the helper: كَيْ نُسَبِّحَكَ كَثِيرًا.

luna: Continuing the purpose in 20:33, this ayah says “وَنَذْكُرَكَ كَثِيرًا”; shared support serves abundant remembrance as well as glorification. | terra: Abundant remembrance completes the stated purpose of Aaron's support and links help, ease, and dhikr in the source image.

luna: After Moses’ requests for a helper, shared work, and remembrance in 20:29–34, God answers “قَدْ أُوتِيتَ سُؤْلَكَ”; this neighbor completes the image by showing the plea granted. | terra: God's “You have been granted your request, Moses” confirms that the Lord supplies the requested ease and helper.
terra: God sends Moses and his brother together and tells them not to slacken in His remembrance, joining granted partnership to the prayer's dhikr purpose.
terra: The people say they were made to carry أَوْزَارًا of ornaments and then cast them, a physical-load use of the source root distinct from moral burden.

luna: This ayah names turning away from God’s reminder; its next neighbor, 20:101, calls the consequence a load borne on Judgment Day, contrasting the relieved burden with one accumulated by rejecting remembrance. | terra: One who turns from the Reminder will carry a وِزْرًا on Resurrection Day, preserving the source root's burden sense and its bearer relation.

luna: Following 20:100’s turning away from the reminder, this ayah says “وَسَاءَ لَهُمْ يَوْمَ الْقِيَامَةِ حِمْلًا,” a burden carried at judgment rather than one removed by God. | terra: The burden of 20:100 remains with them, and this ayah calls it an evil load on Resurrection Day; it completes what that wizr does to its bearer.
terra: The Prophet is told to endure hostile speech and glorify his Lord throughout the day, another strain-to-tasbih movement in the same surah as Moses' minister prayer.
terra: The question asks whether they possess gods that can protect them from God, then denies those gods can help themselves or enjoy His protection.
luna: The section depicts God removing a load from the addressee; Job calls to his Lord from affliction and says that harm has touched him, identifying the plea whose answer in 21:84 removes it.
luna: Answering Job’s affliction in 21:83, this ayah says God responded and removed his harm, a direct parallel to the burden being taken away.
luna: The section’s refuge image ends in turning to the Rabb; Jonah calls to God from darkness, admitting his wrong, which is a concrete appeal from distress toward the only refuge.
luna: Answering Jonah’s call in 21:87, this ayah says God rescued him from distress and does likewise for believers, directly joining appeal to God with release from a burden.
terra: God places no hardship in the religion and commands believers to hold fast to Him, then names Himself their excellent Protector and Helper; relief and refuge are inseparable here.
terra: God charges no soul beyond capacity and keeps a truthful record, combining a bounded load with exact accountability.
terra: The Prophet is taught to say, “My Lord, I seek refuge in You” from the devils' incitements, joining the refuge act explicitly to Rabb.
terra: He also seeks refuge in his Lord from the devils' very presence, completing the two-part shelter prayer.
terra: The Messenger bears what he is charged with and the audience bears what it is charged with, assigning each party's task without transferring it.

luna: The section develops Moses’ request for a family helper, and this ayah says Aaron was made “وَزِيرًا” alongside him; it shows the requested burden-sharing role put into place. | terra: God says He appointed Aaron as a وَزِيرًا with Moses, directly answering the minister image with divine provision.
terra: God sends both Moses and Aaron to the denying people, showing the shared mission for which the minister of 25:35 was appointed.

luna: The section’s root note presents a backer as support for a master and ends by turning to the true Rabb; this ayah says the disbeliever is “عَلَىٰ رَبِّهِ ظَهِيرًا,” a reversal in which support is set against one’s Lord. | terra: The rejecter is a ظَهِيرًا against his Lord, turning the supporting-back relation toward the wrong side.
terra: Moses tells his Lord that his breast tightens and his tongue does not flow, grounding the request for Aaron in 26:13.

luna: The section links an opened chest and an eased task with Moses’ request for Aaron; in this parallel prayer his chest narrows and he asks, “فَأَرْسِلْ إِلَىٰ هَارُونَ,” showing the helper answers a constricted speaker’s need. | terra: Moses' constricted breast and speech difficulty lead directly to “send for Aaron,” restaging the need from which the supporting brother is requested.
terra: Moses fears retaliation for an earlier offense; this ayah adds danger, beyond speech difficulty, to his need for divine and fraternal support.
terra: God answers the request by sending both brothers with His signs and assuring them of His hearing presence, so divine support underwrites human partnership.
terra: Pharaoh says to Moses, “Did we not rear you among us as a child?”; نُرَبِّكَ activates the root's nurture and setting-right sense while exposing a tyrant's claim on the servant.
terra: Pharaoh asks his chiefs what they advise regarding Moses, staging a ruler's reliance on a council, albeit within a hostile cause.
terra: The chiefs recommend delaying Moses and Aaron and gathering magicians, supplying the counsel requested by the ruler in 26:35.
terra: When the two groups come into view, Moses' companions think they have been overtaken; this is the crisis of failed outward escape answered by reliance on the Lord in 26:62.
terra: Moses rejects despair because “my Lord is with me; He will guide me,” making the Lord Himself the support when no visible refuge remains.
terra: The people skillfully carve houses from mountains, repeating the built mountain shelter but without 15:82's explicit security term.
terra: The queen asks her chiefs for counsel and refuses to decide an affair without their presence, exactly staging the source definition of a ruler relying on advisers' judgment.
terra: The chiefs offer strength and force but leave the command to the queen, completing 27:32's ruler-and-counsellors scene while preserving her authority.

luna: The section’s dictionary root ظ ه ر names a helper or backer; after the killing, Moses vows “فَلَنْ أَكُونَ ظَهِيرًا لِّلْمُجْرِمِينَ,” setting a moral boundary on whom he will support. | terra: Moses vows never to be a ظَهِيرًا for criminals, marking the moral boundary on whom one's supporting back may uphold.
terra: Moses recalls killing one of Pharaoh's people and fears being killed, the concrete peril immediately preceding his request for Aaron as support.

luna: The section develops a helper who shares another’s task; Moses asks Pharaoh to send Aaron as “رِدْءًا يُصَدِّقُنِي,” a support who can stand with and confirm him. | terra: Moses asks for Aaron as a رِدْءًا who will confirm him, a precise nonlexical formulation of the supporting minister.

luna: The section’s helper leans in to strengthen another; God answers Moses, “سَنَشُدُّ عَضُدَكَ بِأَخِيكَ,” promising strength through his brother. | terra: God answers, “We shall strengthen your arm through your brother,” turning fraternal aid into the same bodily support image as the braced back.
terra: The opponents call Moses' and Aaron's revelations “two sorceries supporting one another,” preserving the root's mutual-backing sense inside hostile speech.
terra: Korah has no faction to help him against Allah and cannot help himself when the earth swallows him, a failed human “back.”
terra: The Prophet is commanded not to be a ظَهِيرًا for the rejecters, repeating the ethical boundary on support found in Moses' vow.
terra: Rejecters promise believers, “We will carry your sins,” but the ayah denies that they can carry any of them, exposing a false offer to act as burden-bearer.

luna: The section’s helper bears another’s weight to relieve him; this ayah says the misleaders carry “أَثْقَالًا مَّعَ أَثْقَالِهِمْ,” showing that sharing another’s burden can instead increase it when one leads them astray. | terra: The misleaders will bear their own loads and further loads with them, showing acquired responsibility for misleading rather than substitution for another bearer.

luna: The section’s broad refuge gloss concerns what one fortifies oneself with; this ayah likens false protectors taken besides God to a spider’s house, making an apparent shelter’s weakness visible. | terra: Taking protectors besides Allah is compared to the spider taking a house, the frailty of the shelter exposing false refuge.
terra: Neither parent can avail child nor child parent before the Lord, contrasting the effective brotherly aid of Aaron with kinship's limit in final accountability.
terra: The Prophet is told that flight will not benefit anyone fleeing death or killing, placing a limit on escape as refuge.
terra: No one can shield people from Allah if He intends harm or withhold His mercy, and they find no protector or helper apart from Him.
terra: The People of the Book who backed the confederates are brought down from their fortresses, joining wrongful support with a failed stronghold.
terra: Believers are commanded to remember Allah with abundant remembrance, the same stated purpose for which Moses asks a supporting brother.
terra: They are also commanded to glorify Him morning and evening, completing the dhikr–tasbih pair begun in 33:41.
terra: Women are told to draw their outer garments around themselves so they may be recognized and not harmed, a protective-clothing parallel to the source's girded-garment branch.
terra: The heavens, earth, and mountains shrink from bearing the Trust, while the human undertakes it; the scene tests what can carry a weight rather than merely shelter from it.
terra: False gods own no share in creation and God has no ظَهِيرٍ among them, denying that the sovereign Lord requires the kind of supporting minister a ruler needs.

luna: The section describes a helper carrying a burden off someone; this ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى” and that even a heavily laden soul’s plea brings none of its burden onto another, a direct limit on human load-sharing. | terra: A heavily laden soul may call even a close relative to its load, yet none of it is carried; this is the sharpest reversal of the kin-minister who takes another's weight.
terra: Two messengers are reinforced with a third when rejected, a precise narrative instance of adding a person to brace a difficult mission.
terra: People take gods besides Allah hoping to be helped, locating the error precisely in seeking support from false masters.
terra: Those gods cannot help their devotees; instead the devotees are mustered as troops for them, reversing who supports whom.
terra: God's favor is explicitly bestowed on Moses and Aaron together, framing their partnership as provision from the Lord.
terra: God rescues both brothers and their people from great distress, continuing the Lord's supporting action toward the paired servants.
terra: God helps Moses and Aaron until they prevail, making divine aid the ground of the brothers' successful shared mission.
luna: The section images the Rabb relieving a servant’s burden; in this repeated account Job calls his Lord because Satan has touched him with exhaustion and suffering, a specific plea under a load.
luna: Following Job’s plea in 38:41, this ayah gives him a spring and cold drink by God’s command, showing the practical relief that answers the affliction.
luna: After the relief in 38:42, this neighbor says God restored Job’s family and more as mercy and reminder; it completes the account of the Lord’s response to the burden described in 38:41.

luna: The section joins a removed وِزْر to turning toward the Rabb; this ayah says “وَلَا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى” and later “ثُمَّ إِلَىٰ رَبِّكُم مَّرْجِعُكُمْ,” pairing personal responsibility with return to the Lord. | terra: No bearer carries another's burden and all return to their Lord, placing nontransferable accountability beside the section's Lordward destination.

luna: The section connects Moses’ request for an opened chest with a difficult task; this ayah depicts a person whose chest God opens to Islam and who is then on light from his Lord, a direct parallel for the image of inward opening.
terra: “Is Allah not sufficient for His servant?” states the source section's reversal plainly: the Lord bears up the servant rather than needing a minister.
terra: Moses seeks refuge in “my Lord and your Lord” from every arrogant person who denies reckoning, adding his own explicit Lordward refuge stance.
terra: On the day people turn in flight, they have no protector from Allah; the attempted escape ends without a human or material backer.
terra: The repeated instruction to seek refuge in Allah from satanic incitement presents God as the immediate protector in an inward threat.
terra: Humans cannot escape in the earth and have no protector or helper apart from Allah, combining failed flight with failed backing.

luna: The section’s minister is a person relied on for judgment; this ayah describes believers conducting their affairs by consultation among themselves, a collective form of the counsel relation developed in the dictionary note. | terra: The believers conduct their affair by mutual consultation, paralleling both counsel relied upon and Moses' request that Aaron share in his affair.
terra: The command to answer the Lord precedes a day with no مَلْجَإٍ, matching the Last-Day denial of refuge while directing response to God.
terra: On the Day, no patron can avail another and none are helped except those shown mercy, bounding interpersonal support by the Lord's mercy.
terra: The Quran is made easy in the Prophet's tongue so that people may remember, again joining eased utterance to remembrance.
terra: حَتَّىٰ تَضَعَ الْحَرْبُ أَوْزَارَهَا joins “laying down” with the same burden root, an exact lexical echo in the distinct idiom of war ending.
terra: “If you support Allah, He will support you and make your feet firm” sets creaturely service and divine strengthening in a reciprocal relation.
terra: Allah is the مَوْلَى of the believers whereas the rejecters have no protector, defining the Lord–servant relation through active protection.
terra: God's forgiveness of the Prophet's earlier and later fault and completion of favor is a concrete same-addressee instance of the Lord removing what weighs upon His servant.
terra: God promises the Prophet a mighty support immediately after forgiveness and completed favor, joining burden relief to divine backing.
terra: If the rejecters fought, they would turn their backs and find neither protector nor helper, making the physical back part of the failure of support.
terra: A crop's shoot strengthens it—فَآزَرَهُ—giving a concrete Quranic image for the separate أ ز ر root used in Moses' “strengthen my back,” not the و ز ر burden root.

luna: The section ends with the addressee’s turning to the Rabb; this command, “فَفِرُّوا إِلَى اللَّهِ,” makes that movement an urgent flight toward God. | terra: “Flee to Allah” turns the refuge image into a command of directed flight, matching the section's movement toward the Lord.
terra: The Prophet is told to endure his Lord's judgment because he is “before Our eyes,” then to glorify his Lord; protection and tasbih occur in one address.
terra: Night glorification continues the protected tasbih command of 52:48 and completes that passage's temporal scope.

luna: The section’s root note connects وِزْر with a carried load; the ayah states “أَلَّا تَزِرُ وَازِرَةٌ وِزْرَ أُخْرَى,” the boundary that no one carries another’s guilt. | terra: The scrolls of Moses and Abraham affirm that no bearer bears another's burden, a scriptural boundary on the Moses–Aaron minister image.
luna: The burden rule in 53:38 continues here: “وَأَن لَّيْسَ لِلْإِنسَانِ إِلَّا مَا سَعَى” says each person has only what they strove for, clarifying the personal load that cannot be shifted.
luna: Continuing the personal-accountability statement of 53:38–39, this ayah says “وَأَنَّ سَعْيَهُ سَوْفَ يُرَىٰ”; each person’s own striving is made visible before its recompense.

luna: After 53:38’s no-transfer rule and the next two ayat on each person’s striving, this neighbor says “ثُمَّ يُجْزَاهُ الْجَزَاءَ الْأَوْفَىٰ,” completing the account of an individual’s burden and result.
terra: “To your Lord is the final end” repeats the section's exact Lordward direction and presents Him as the terminus after all other recourse ends.
terra: “We made the Quran easy for remembrance” joins the two successive aims in Moses' prayer—ease and dhikr—in one repeated formula.
terra: The repeated claim that the Quran is made easy for remembrance reinforces facilitation as a means to remembering God.
terra: This third refrain again links what God makes easy with the human act of taking reminder.
terra: The final refrain preserves the surah-wide repetition of divinely made ease for remembrance.
terra: The expelled people thought their fortresses would protect them from Allah, but their constructed refuge failed from an unexpected direction.
terra: A mountain would humble and split if the Quran descended upon it, unsettling the mountain's appearance as an unshakable refuge or bearer.

luna: The section develops a backer as someone who stands with another; here people “ظَاهَرُوا عَلَىٰ إِخْرَاجِكُمْ” by aiding your expulsion, a hostile use of support that marks its boundary. | terra: Those who support others in expelling believers are placed outside permitted allegiance, another moral boundary on whom one backs.
terra: Believers are told to be helpers of Allah as Jesus' disciples were; the supported party then becomes ظَاهِرِينَ, linking aid to the root's distinct prevailing sense.
terra: The donkey carrying books is a bearer that gains nothing from its load, a negative boundary on equating mere load-carrying with the purposeful help of a minister.
terra: The death from which people flee will inevitably meet them, another direct boundary on physical escape.
terra: Whoever relies upon Allah finds Him sufficient, directly expressing the minister image's dependence and shelter with God as its true object.
terra: God charges no soul beyond what He has given it and promises ease after hardship, combining measured burden with the promise central to surah 94.

luna: The section defines ظَهِير as a helper, as if one back rested against another; this ayah calls the angels “ظَهِيرٌ” for the Prophet after naming Allah his protector, while the wives’ mutual backing had opposed him. | terra: Allah, Gabriel, and the righteous believers stand with the Prophet, and the angels are a ظَهِيرٌ; this directly realizes the source dictionary's “back” as helper.

luna: The section ends by directing the addressee toward the Rabb as refuge; Pharaoh’s wife asks her Lord for a home near Him and deliverance from Pharaoh and his deeds, a concrete flight from an earthly ruler to divine shelter.
terra: The question asks what army could help anyone besides the Merciful, denying an alternative body of supporters.

luna: The section says its root’s broad refuge sense covers what one hides in or fortifies oneself with; the speaker says no one can protect him from God and “وَلَن أَجِدَ مِن دُونِهِ مُلْتَحَدًا,” ruling out refuge elsewhere. | terra: The Messenger says no one can protect him from Allah and he can find no مُلْتَحَدًا apart from Him, closely paralleling the section's no-refuge-except-to-Him claim.
terra: God will cast a “weighty word” upon the Prophet, a specific counterpoint to the burden He removes and the task He eases.
terra: “Remember the name of your Lord” and devote yourself wholly to Him gives the Lordward remembrance for which Moses sought supporting partnership.
terra: The next ayah identifies the Lord of east and west and commands, “take Him as guardian,” making reliance the consequence of the remembrance in 73:8.
terra: God knows the community cannot sustain the full night measure, turns toward them, and repeatedly permits whatever recitation is easy, concretely reducing a devotional load.

luna: The section links a burden’s release to refuge in the Rabb; here the person asks “أَيْنَ الْمَفَرُّ,” and the next ayah 75:11 answers that there is no refuge, so this row contributes the search that prompts the answer. | terra: The human cry “Where is the escape?” opens the exact refuge scene answered by لَا وَزَرَ in 75:11.

luna: The section’s dictionary root و ز ر includes a mountain refuge, while this ayah answers the search for escape with “لَا وَزَرَ” (no refuge); it gives the named shelter a stark limit at judgment. | terra: لَا وَزَرَ uses the same و ز ر root in its “mountain/refuge” sense and denies any such shelter on the Last Day.

luna: The section ends by turning toward the Rabb; this ayah says “إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ” is the destination that day, joining refuge to the return to one’s Lord. | terra: إِلَىٰ رَبِّكَ names the Lord as the only final destination immediately after refuge is denied, exactly joining the section's source root and closing direction.
terra: Later in the same refuge-denying surah, “to your Lord that day is the driving” restates the unavoidable destination first named in 75:12.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to remember the name of his Lord morning and evening, matching the remembrance enabled by Moses' requested support.
terra: Night prostration and prolonged glorification complete the remembrance-and-tasbih pair begun in 76:25.

luna: The section identifies Rabb as the obeyed master and directs the addressee to the Rabb; Pharaoh’s claim “أَنَا رَبُّكُمُ الْأَعْلَىٰ” is the opposing, false claim to that authority. | terra: Pharaoh's claim “I am your highest lord” is the tyrant's counterfeit of the master-title that belongs to God.
terra: On that Day a person flees from his brother, a pointed reversal of Moses seeking his brother as his supporting minister.
terra: The human is described as laboring toward the Lord until meeting Him, joining strenuous work to the Lordward direction that follows work in surah 94.
terra: “Glorify the name of your Lord, the Most High” directs the same praise toward the Lord to whom the servant finally turns.
terra: God tells the Prophet, “We shall ease you toward ease,” a same-addressee promise of divine facilitation.
terra: The reassured soul is commanded to return to its Lord, a fulfilled and peaceful form of the section's final turning.
terra: The generous, God-fearing believer is facilitated toward ease, showing ease as a divinely prepared course.
terra: God facilitates the miserly denier toward hardship, the dark counterpart to divinely granted ease in Moses' prayer and surah 94.

luna: Like the section’s addressee receiving relief and a place to turn, the earlier address says God found him an orphan and “فَآوَىٰ” (gave shelter), a direct scene of divine refuge. | terra: The same divine speaker reminds the Prophet that He found him an orphan and gave shelter, a direct instance of the Lord as the servant's refuge.
terra: “To your Lord is the return” repeats the section's closing direction while correcting the human illusion of self-sufficiency in the preceding ayat.
terra: The arrival of Allah's help supplies the enabling support whose response is glorification in 110:3.
terra: After divine help and victory, the Prophet is commanded to glorify his Lord and seek forgiveness, echoing support ordered toward tasbih.
terra: The Prophet is commanded to seek refuge in the Lord of daybreak, directly joining the act of taking shelter to rabb, the section's closing title.
terra: The command to seek refuge in the Lord of humankind is an exact Lordward refuge stance.
terra: “King of humankind” immediately explains the sovereign-master dimension of the Rabb invoked as refuge in 114:1.
